<<군인사법 제7조(의무복무기간)>> ① 장교, 준사관 및 부사관(지원에 의하지 아니하고 임용된 하사는 제외한다)의 의무복무기간은 다음 각 호와 같다. 다만, 전시ㆍ사변 등의 국가비상시에는 예외로 한다. <개정 2012. 12. 18., 2014. 3. 11., 2020. 12. 22.>

1. 장기복무 장교의 의무복무기간은 10년으로 한다. 다만, 장기복무 장교로 임용된 날부터 5년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역(轉役)을 지원할 수 있다.

2. 제1호에도 불구하고 해군의 장교 또는 공군의 장교로서 비행훈련과정을 수료하여 비행자격을 취득한 사람[회전익(回轉翼)항공기로 기종이 분류된 사람은 제외한다] 중 해군사관학교 또는 공군사관학교를 졸업한 사람의 의무복무기간은 15년, 그 외의 사람의 의무복무기간은 13년으로 한다. 다만, 장교로 임용된 날부터 5년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역을 지원할 수 있다.

3. 국방부장관은 인력 운영을 위하여 필요하다고 인정하는 경우에는 2년의 범위에서 제2호에 따른 의무복무기간을 단축할 수 있다.

4. 단기복무 장교의 의무복무기간은 3년으로 한다. 다만, 육군3사관학교나 국군간호사관학교를 졸업한 사람은 6년으로 하고, 「병역법」 제57조제2항에 따른 학생군사교육단 사관후보생과정 출신 장교, 여군(女軍) 중 간호과 장교(국군간호사관학교를 졸업한 간호과 장교는 제외한다) 및 예비역 장교로서 전역 당시의 계급에 재임용된 중위 이상의 장교에 대하여는 국방부장관이 각 군의 인력 운영을 위하여 필요하다고 인정하는 경우 1년의 범위에서 그 복무기간을 단축할 수 있다.

5. 준사관의 의무복무기간은 5년으로 한다. 다만, 대통령령으로 정하는 군의 필수 기술 분야에 종사하는 준사관(상사와 원사에서 준사관으로 임용된 사람은 제외한다)은 10년으로 하되, 임용된 날부터 7년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역을 지원할 수 있다.

6. 장기복무 부사관의 의무복무기간은 7년으로 한다. 다만, 대통령령으로 정하는 군의 필수 기술 분야에 종사하는 장기복무 부사관은 10년으로 하되, 장기복무 부사관으로 임용된 날부터 7년이 되는 해에 한 차례 전역을 지원할 수 있다.

7. 단기복무 부사관의 의무복무기간은 4년으로 하되, 다음 각 목의 어느 하나에 해당하는 단기복무 부사관의 의무복무기간은 다음 각 목의 구분에 따른다.

가. 제6조제7항제3호의 단기복무 부사관: 「병역법」 제20조의2제1항에 따른 임기

나. 삭제 <2016. 12. 20.>

다. 제6조제7항제5호의 단기복무 부사관: 「병역법」 제18조 및 제19조에 따른 병의 복무기간

라. 제6조제7항제6호의 단기복무 부사관: 3년. 다만, 국방부장관은 인력 운영을 위하여 필요하다고 인정하는 경우에는 1년의 범위에서 그 복무기간을 단축할 수 있다.

② 군인으로서 위탁교육이나 그 밖의 교육을 받은 사람은 다음 각 호의 구분에 따른 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산(加算)하여 복무한다. 이 경우 가산하여 복무할 기간은 의무복무 연한(年限) 내에 교육을 마친 경우에는 그 의무복무 연한 만료일의 다음 날부터 계산하고, 의무복무 연한이 지난 후에 교육을 마친 경우에는 그 교육이 끝난 날의 다음 날부터 계산한다. <개정 2023. 10. 31.>

1. 외국에서 6개월 이상 위탁교육을 받은 사람: 그 교육기간의 2배에 상당하는 기간

2. 국내의 군 외의 교육기관에서 6개월 이상 위탁교육을 받은 사람: 그 교육기간에 상당하는 기간

3. 국내의 군 교육기관에서 학위과정의 교육을 6개월 이상 받은 사람: 그 교육기간에 상당하는 기간

4. 국내에서 주간 근무를 하면서 일과 후 6개월 이상 또는 주말에 6개월 이상 위탁교육을 받은 사람: 그 교육기간의 2분의 1에 상당하는 기간

③ 의무장교로서 기초의학과정이나 전문의학과정을 수습(修習)한 사람은 그 수습기간에 상당하는 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무한다.

④ 제62조제1항에 따라 선발되어 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 사람으로서 단기복무 장교로 임용된 사람은 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 기간에 상당하는 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무한다. 다만, 국방부장관은 제62조제1항에 따라 선발되어 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 사람으로서 부사관으로 임용된 사람에게는 그 의무복무기간에 군 가산복무 지원금을 받은 기간 이내의 기간을 가산하여 복무하도록 할 수 있다. <개정 2012. 3. 21., 2017. 3. 21.>

⑤ 국방부장관은 특수장비를 운용하기 위하여 외국에서 위탁교육을 받은 사람에게는 다음 각 호의 구분에 따른 기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무하도록 할 수 있다. 이 경우 그 가산 방법은 제2항에 따른다.

1. 그 이수기간의 2배에 해당하는 기간이 3년 미만인 경우: 3년까지

2. 그 이수기간의 2배에 해당하는 기간이 3년을 넘는 경우: 그 교육기간의 2배에 해당하는 기간

⑥ 제6조제4항 또는 제8항에 따라 전형을 거쳐 복무기간이 연장된 단기복무 장교 또는 단기복무 부사관은 그 연장된 복무기간을 의무복무기간에 가산하여 복무한다. <신설 2021. 4. 13.>

[전문개정 2011. 5. 24.]

<<군위탁생규정 제12조(지급경비의 반납조치)>> ①각군 참모총장은 군위탁생으로서 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 사람에 대해서는 제6조에 따라 지급받은 경비(이하 이 조에서 “지급경비”라 한다)를 별표의 기준에 따라 반납하도록 해야 하고, 본인이 반납하지 않는 경우에는 그의 보증인(「보험업법」에 따라 보증보험 증권을 발행한 보험회사를 포함한다. 이하 같다)에게 보증채무의 이행을 청구해야 한다. 다만, 지급경비의 환수가 곤란하거나 면제할 필요가 있을 때에는 각군 참모총장은 국방부장관의 승인(준사관 및 부사관의 경우는 제외한다)을 받아 반납을 6개월의 범위에서 연기하거나 그 일부 또는 전부의 반납을 면제할 수 있다. <개정 1995. 12. 22., 2001. 3. 27., 2019. 5. 28., 2021. 4. 20.>

1. 소정의 과정을 마친 후 정당한 사유 없이 복귀하지 아니한 사람

2. 수학 중 해임된 사람. 다만, 제10조제1항제1호(제5조제5호에 따른 결격사유로 한정한다) 또는 제11조에 해당하는 경우는 제외한다.

3. 소정의 과정을 마친 후 의무복무기간 중에 전역 또는 제적 등의 사유가 발생하여 복무의무를 이행하지 않은 사람

4. 교육결과보고서(제11조의2제3항에 따른 교육성과 자료를 포함한다. 이하 이 항에서 같다)의 내용이 교육목적을 달성하지 못한 것으로 평가된 사람

5. 다른 보고서 또는 논문 등을 표절하여 교육결과보고서를 제출한 사람

6. 교육결과보고서를 기한 내에 제출하지 못한 사람

7. 교육 과정이 학위 과정인 경우 학위를 취득하지 못한 사람

② 각군 참모총장은 제1항 각 호 외의 부분 본문에 따라 지급경비를 반납하게 할 경우에는 반납의무자에게 지급경비반납통고서를 보내야 한다. <개정 2019. 5. 28.>

③제1항 각 호 외의 부분 단서에 따라 지급경비의 반납을 연기하거나 면제받으려는 군위탁생 또는 그 보증인은 반납원인이 발생한 날부터 1개월 이내에 지급경비반납연기(면제)신청서를 소속군 참모총장에게 제출해야 한다. <신설 1995. 12. 22., 2021. 4. 20.>

④각군 참모총장은 반납의무자가 제2항의 규정에 의한 지급경비반납통고서를 받은 날 또는 제3항의 규정에 의한 반납연기기간이 끝난 날부터 90일이내에 지급경비를 납부하지 아니한 때에는 관할세무서장에게 이의 징수를 의뢰하여야 한다. <신설 1995. 12. 22.>

<<군위탁생규정 제12조의2(지급경비의 정산)>> ①각군 참모총장은 제6조의 규정에 의하여 지급한 경비에 대하여 정산사유가 발생한 때에는 관계증빙서류에 의하여 정산하여야 한다.

②제1항의 규정에 의한 정산에 관하여 필요한 사항은 국방부장관이 정한다.

[본조신설 1995. 12. 22.]

<<군위탁생규정  제6조(경비등의 지급)>> ①군위탁생에 대하여는 수학기간중 입학금ㆍ등록금 기타 필요한 경비를 지급한다.

②국외위탁생에 대하여는 왕복항공료 및 체재비를 지급하며, 6개월 이상 수학하는 국외위탁생에 대하여는 배우자 및 자녀의 왕복항공료, 의료보험료 또는 의료보조비, 생활준비금 및 귀국이전비를 가산하여 지급할 수 있다. 이 경우 체재비의 지급액은 월 단위로 계산하되, 월 미만의 일수에 대하여는 월 기준일을 30일로 하여 날 수에 비례하여 계산한다. <개정 2009. 10. 19.>

③군위탁생에 대한 제1항 및 제2항의 경비의 지급범위 및 지급액은 예산의 범위안에서 국방부장관이 정한다.

<<국가재정법 제96조(금전채권ㆍ채무의 소멸시효)>> ①금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 국가의 권리로서 시효에 관하여 다른 법률에 규정이 없는 것은 5년 동안 행사하지 아니하면 시효로 인하여 소멸한다.

②국가에 대한 권리로서 금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 것도 또한 제1항과 같다.

③금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 국가의 권리의 경우 소멸시효의 중단ㆍ정지 그 밖의 사항에 관하여 다른 법률의 규정이 없는 때에는 「민법」의 규정을 적용한다. 국가에 대한 권리로서 금전의 급부를 목적으로 하는 것도 또한 같다. <개정 2020. 6. 9.>

④법령의 규정에 따라 국가가 행하는 납입의 고지는 시효중단의 효력이 있다.

<<민법 제166조(소멸시효의 기산점)>> ①소멸시효는 권리를 행사할 수 있는 때로부터 진행한다.

②부작위를 목적으로 하는 채권의 소멸시효는 위반행위를 한 때로부터 진행한다.

context:
The robust framework governing financial reporting and audit oversight within the United States and the European Union is designed to uphold market integrity, protect investors, and ensure the reliability of financial information. In the United States, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX) stands as a landmark piece of legislation, establishing the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) under the oversight of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The PCAOB is entrusted with the critical mission of overseeing the audits of public companies to protect investors. Its responsibilities include registering public accounting firms, establishing audit standards, conducting inspections of registered firms, and enforcing compliance with SOX and its own rules. For instance, PCAOB Auditing Standard No. 2201, 'An Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting That Is Integrated with An Audit of Financial Statements,' outlines the auditor's responsibilities for integrated audits, directly impacting the scope and depth of an audit engagement and, by extension, the resources, including audit hours, dedicated to achieving audit quality. 

The SEC, through its various regulations, reinforces auditor independence and disclosure requirements. Under Section 201 of SOX, auditors are prohibited from providing certain non-audit services to their audit clients, a measure intended to prevent conflicts of interest and enhance independence. Furthermore, the SEC's rules under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and the Securities Act of 1933 mandate comprehensive financial reporting, including adherence to Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP), which external auditors must attest to. The concept of 'Auditor Designation' in the US context primarily relates to the client's selection of an independent auditor, subject to audit committee approval, rather than direct regulatory assignment, though regulatory bodies like the PCAOB can impose sanctions, including revocation of registration, which effectively prohibits an auditor from practicing. 

In the European Union, the Audit Regulation (EU) No 537/2014 and Directive 2014/56/EU significantly bolster the requirements for statutory audits of public-interest entities (PIEs). These legislative instruments introduce measures such as mandatory audit firm rotation, prohibitions on certain non-audit services, and enhanced reporting requirements for auditors. Article 17 of the Audit Regulation, for example, mandates audit firm rotation for PIEs, generally after a maximum engagement period of ten years, with possibilities for extension under certain conditions. This aims to reinforce auditor independence and inject fresh perspectives into the audit process, directly contributing to Audit Quality. The Directive also strengthens the powers of national competent authorities, such as the UK's Financial Reporting Council (FRC) (now the Audit, Reporting and Governance Authority - ARGA), to oversee auditors and audit firms. These authorities conduct reviews of audit engagements and systems of quality control, taking into account factors like the resources allocated to audits. While the term 'Standard Audit Hours' is not explicitly defined as a regulatory threshold for intervention in the EU legislation, the assessment of sufficient resources for an audit, including time allocation, is a critical component of audit quality reviews conducted by these competent authorities. Insufficient allocation of resources could be a red flag for potential audit deficiencies, leading to supervisory actions. The 'External Audit Act' in this jurisdiction refers collectively to the comprehensive legal framework governing the statutory audit profession and practice, ensuring high standards of professional conduct and robust oversight by bodies akin to a 'Securities and Futures Commission' in their respective remits.

외부감사법 제11조(증권선물위원회에 의한 감사인 지정 등) 
① 증권선물위원회는 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 회사에 3개 사업연도의 범위에서 증권선물위원회가 지정하는 회계법인을 감사인으로 선임하거나 변경선임할 것을 요구할 수 있다.

1. 감사 또는 감사위원회(감사위원회가 설치되지 아니한 주권상장법인, 대형비상장주식회사 또는 금융회사의 경우는 감사인선임위원회를 말한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)의 승인을 받아 제10조에 따른 감사인의 선임기간 내에 증권선물위원회에 감사인 지정을 요청한 회사

2. 제10조에 따른 감사인의 선임기간 내에 감사인을 선임하지 아니한 회사

3. 제10조제3항 또는 제4항을 위반하여 감사인을 선임하거나 증권선물위원회가 회사의 감사인 교체 사유가 부당하다고 인정한 회사

4. 증권선물위원회의 감리 결과 제5조에 따른 회계처리기준을 위반하여 재무제표를 작성한 사실이 확인된 회사. 다만, 증권선물위원회가 정하는 경미한 위반이 확인된 회사는 제외한다.

5. 제6조제6항을 위반하여 회사의 재무제표를 감사인이 대신하여 작성하거나, 재무제표 작성과 관련된 회계처리에 대한 자문을 요구하거나 받은 회사

6. 주권상장법인 중 다음 각 목의 어느 하나에 해당하는 회사

가. 3개 사업연도 연속 영업이익이 0보다 작은 회사

나. 3개 사업연도 연속 영업현금흐름이 0보다 작은 회사

다. 3개 사업연도 연속 이자보상배율이 1 미만인 회사

라. 그 밖에 대통령령으로 정하는 재무기준에 해당하는 회사

7. 주권상장법인 중 대통령령으로 정하는 바에 따라 증권선물위원회가 공정한 감사가 필요하다고 인정하여 지정하는 회사

8. 「기업구조조정 촉진법」 제2조제5호에 따른 주채권은행 또는 대통령령으로 정하는 주주가 대통령령으로 정하는 방법에 따라 증권선물위원회에 감사인 지정을 요청하는 경우의 해당 회사

9. 제13조제1항 또는 제2항을 위반하여 감사계약의 해지 또는 감사인의 해임을 하지 아니하거나 새로운 감사인을 선임하지 아니한 회사

10. 감사인의 감사시간이 제16조의2제1항에서 정하는 표준 감사시간보다 현저히 낮은 수준이라고 증권선물위원회가 인정한 회사

11. 직전 사업연도를 포함하여 과거 3년간 최대주주의 변경이 2회 이상 발생하거나 대표이사의 교체가 3회 이상 발생한 주권상장법인

12. 그 밖에 공정한 감사가 특히 필요하다고 인정되어 대통령령으로 정하는 회사

외부감사법 제10조(감사인의 선임)
⑤ 감사 또는 감사위원회(제4항제2호 단서에 따라 감사인을 선임한 회사는 회사를 대표하는 이사를 말한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)는 감사인의 감사보수와 감사시간, 감사에 필요한 인력에 관한 사항을 문서로 정하여야 한다. 이 경우 감사위원회가 설치되지 아니한 주권상장법인, 대형비상장주식회사 또는 금융회사의 감사는 감사인선임위원회의 승인을 받아야 한다.

⑥ 감사 또는 감사위원회는 제23조제1항에 따라 감사보고서를 제출받은 경우 제5항에서 정한 사항이 준수되었는지를 확인하여야 한다. 이 경우 감사위원회가 설치되지 아니한 주권상장법인, 대형비상장주식회사 또는 금융회사의 감사는 제5항에서 정한 사항이 준수되었는지를 확인한 문서를 감사인선임위원회에 제출하여야 한다.

외부감사법 시행령 제13조(감사인 선정 등)
④ 제3항 전단에 따른 기준에는 다음 각 호의 사항이 포함되어야 한다.

Beyond the transatlantic frameworks, other major financial centers have equally sophisticated regulatory regimes to ensure robust financial reporting and audit quality. In Singapore, the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) serves as the national regulator of business entities, public accountants, and corporate service providers. ACRA’s oversight of public accountants is primarily governed by the Accountants Act, which sets out the requirements for registration, professional conduct, and disciplinary actions against auditors. The Companies Act also contains provisions relating to the appointment, duties, and powers of auditors of Singapore-incorporated companies. ACRA’s robust inspection regime assesses the quality of audit engagements performed by registered public accountants, focusing on compliance with Singapore Standards on Auditing (SSAs) and the Ethical Pronouncements (EPs) issued by the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants (ISCA). A key aspect of these inspections involves evaluating whether audit firms allocate adequate resources, including sufficient 'Standard Audit Hours,' to complex engagements to ensure thoroughness and proper professional skepticism, which are paramount to maintaining Audit Quality. While 'Auditor Designation' is typically client-driven, ACRA has the power to impose conditions, suspend, or cancel an auditor's registration for breaches of professional standards, which could effectively lead to regulatory 'designation' of an inability to practice. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) also plays a crucial role for financial institutions, prescribing stringent internal control and governance requirements that indirectly influence the scope and expectations placed upon external auditors. The collective regulatory statutes and guidelines form Singapore's comprehensive 'External Audit Act' framework, ensuring accountability and transparency in financial reporting. 

In Japan, the Financial Services Agency (FSA) is the primary governmental body responsible for overseeing the financial sector, including audit oversight. Within the FSA, the Certified Public Accountants and Auditing Oversight Board (CPAAOB) is responsible for the inspection of audit firms and certified public accountants, as well as the enforcement of the Certified Public Accountants Act. This Act establishes the legal framework for the auditing profession, including requirements for auditor registration, independence, and professional ethics. The Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), an independent administrative commission under the FSA, functions similarly to a 'Securities and Futures Commission,' monitoring the fairness of securities transactions and ensuring proper disclosure, which includes scrutinizing financial statements and audit reports. The FSA and CPAAOB conduct regular inspections of audit firms, assessing their quality control systems and the execution of individual audit engagements. These inspections often examine the sufficiency of audit procedures performed, which implicitly involves the assessment of 'Standard Audit Hours' and resource allocation. Insufficient time or resources allocated to critical audit areas can be identified as a deficiency impacting overall Audit Quality. The FSA has a strong focus on enhancing the governance of audit firms and promoting a culture of high-quality audits. Where significant deficiencies are identified, the CPAAOB can impose administrative sanctions on audit firms or individual auditors, including business suspension or revocation of registration, which acts as a form of 'Auditor Designation' in a disciplinary context, preventing them from performing audits. This comprehensive regulatory approach underscores the commitment to investor protection and market integrity across these diverse jurisdictions.

Under the U.S. Securities Exchange Act of 1934, broker-dealers are subject to comprehensive regulatory oversight by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Rule 15c3-1 establishes minimum net capital requirements for broker-dealers to ensure financial stability and protect customer assets. The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) Rule 2111 requires member firms to have a reasonable basis to believe that a recommended transaction or investment strategy is suitable for the customer based on information obtained through reasonable diligence.

자본시장법 제172조(내부자의 단기매매차익 반환)
① 주권상장법인의 임원(「상법」 제401조의2제1항 각 호의 자를 포함한다. 이하 이 장에서 같다), 직원(직무상 제174조제1항의 미공개중요정보를 알 수 있는 자로서 대통령령으로 정하는 자에 한한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다) 또는 주요주주가 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 금융투자상품(이하 “특정증권등”이라 한다)을 매수(권리 행사의 상대방이 되는 경우로서 매수자의 지위를 가지게 되는 특정증권등의 매도를 포함한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)한 후 6개월 이내에 매도(권리를 행사할 수 있는 경우로서 매도자의 지위를 가지게 되는 특정증권등의 매수를 포함한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)하거나 특정증권등을 매도한 후 6개월 이내에 매수하여 이익을 얻은 경우에는 그 법인은 그 임직원 또는 주요주주에게 그 이익(이하 “단기매매차익”이라 한다)을 그 법인에게 반환할 것을 청구할 수 있다. 이 경우 이익의 산정기준·반환절차 등에 관하여 필요한 사항은 대통령령으로 정한다.

1. 그 법인이 발행한 증권(대통령령으로 정하는 증권을 제외한다)

2. 제1호의 증권과 관련된 증권예탁증권

3. 그 법인 외의 자가 발행한 것으로서 제1호 또는 제2호의 증권과 교환을 청구할 수 있는 교환사채권

4. 제1호부터 제3호까지의 증권만을 기초자산으로 하는 금융투자상품

자본시장법 제9조(그 밖의 용어의 정의) 
⑪ 이 법에서 “인수”란 제삼자에게 증권을 취득시킬 목적으로 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 행위를 하거나 그 행위를 전제로 발행인 또는 매출인을 위하여 증권의 모집·사모·매출을 하는 것을 말한다. <개정 2013. 5. 28.>

1. 그 증권의 전부 또는 일부를 취득하거나 취득하는 것을 내용으로 하는 계약을 체결하는 것

2. 그 증권의 전부 또는 일부에 대하여 이를 취득하는 자가 없는 때에 그 나머지를 취득하는 것을 내용으로 하는 계약을 체결하는 것

자본시장법 시행령 제198조(단기매매차익 반환의 예외) 법 제172조제6항에서 “대통령령으로 정하는 경우”란 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 경우를 말한다. <개정 2010. 12. 7., 2013. 8. 27., 2019. 6. 25.>
1. 법령에 따라 불가피하게 매수하거나 매도하는 경우

2. 정부의 허가ㆍ인가ㆍ승인 등이나 문서에 의한 지도ㆍ권고에 따라 매수하거나 매도하는 경우

3. 안정조작이나 시장조성을 위하여 매수ㆍ매도 또는 매도ㆍ매수하는 경우

4. 모집ㆍ사모ㆍ매출하는 특정증권등의 인수에 따라 취득하거나 인수한 특정증권등을 처분하는 경우

5. 주식매수선택권의 행사에 따라 주식을 취득하는 경우

6. 이미 소유하고 있는 지분증권, 신주인수권이 표시된 것, 전환사채권 또는 신주인수권부사채권의 권리행사에 따라 주식을 취득하는 경우

7. 법 제172조제1항제2호에 따른 증권예탁증권의 예탁계약 해지에 따라 법 제172조제1항제1호에 따른 증권을 취득하는 경우

8. 법 제172조제1항제1호에 따른 증권 중 제196조제1호라목에 따른 교환사채권 또는 법 제172조제1항제3호에 따른 교환사채권의 권리행사에 따라 증권을 취득하는 경우

9. 모집ㆍ매출하는 특정증권등의 청약에 따라 취득하는 경우

10. 「근로자복지기본법」 제32조에 따라 우리사주조합원에게 우선 배정된 주식의 청약에 따라 취득하는 경우

11. 주식매수청구권의 행사에 따라 주식을 처분하는 경우

12. 공개매수에 응모함에 따라 주식등을 처분하는 경우

13. 그 밖에 미공개중요정보를 이용할 염려가 없는 경우로서 증권선물위원회가 인정하는 경우

context:
The robust framework for Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (CFT) compliance across leading global financial centers mandates stringent data retention policies for financial institutions. These policies are critical for supporting ongoing monitoring, facilitating investigations by competent authorities, and ensuring that institutions can demonstrate their adherence to regulatory obligations through comprehensive audit trails. The scope of data to be retained is extensive, encompassing all information gathered during the customer due diligence (CDD) process, transaction records, and internal analyses related to suspicious activity.

In the United States, the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), administered by the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), establishes foundational requirements for financial institutions to maintain records. Specifically, 31 CFR Chapter X, which details FinCEN’s regulations, outlines various recordkeeping obligations. For instance, 31 CFR § 1010.430 requires financial institutions to retain records of certain funds transfers, while 31 CFR § 1020.220 mandates the establishment of a Customer Identification Program (CIP) that includes procedures for making and maintaining records of the information used to verify a customer's identity. Generally, these records, including those related to Currency Transaction Reports (CTRs), Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), and other BSA-mandated reports, must be retained for a period of five years. This five-year retention period typically commences from the date of the record's creation or, in the case of a SAR, from the date of filing. The purpose of this retention is multifaceted: it enables law enforcement agencies to trace illicit funds, provides a historical record for financial institutions to manage their AML/CFT risks, and serves as evidence of compliance during regulatory examinations. Financial institutions must ensure that these records are readily retrievable and securely stored, protecting them against unauthorized access or alteration, while also being accessible to regulators upon request.

Moving to the European Union, the framework is primarily governed by the Fourth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive (EU) 2015/849, commonly known as 4AMLD), as amended by the Fifth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive (EU) 2018/843, 5AMLD). Article 40 of 4AMLD, titled 'Retention of documents and information,' explicitly addresses data retention requirements. It stipulates that Member States shall require obliged entities to retain the following documents and information: (a) documents and information obtained pursuant to the customer due diligence process, including copies of the identification documents or information equivalent to the copies, for a period of five years after the end of the business relationship with the customer or after the date of an occasional transaction; and (b) records of transactions, consisting of the original documents or copies admissible in court proceedings, for a period of five years after the carrying out of the transactions. The Directive further clarifies that after the expiry of the five-year period, Member States must ensure that obliged entities delete the personal data, unless otherwise provided for by national law, which determines under which circumstances obliged entities may or shall retain data for a longer period. Such longer retention periods are typically justified by the need for the prevention, detection, or investigation of money laundering or terrorist financing, and must be subject to appropriate safeguards. The 5AMLD introduced amendments to Article 40, emphasizing the need for robust data protection measures in line with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) while extending the scope to new obliged entities and enhancing beneficial ownership transparency. Financial institutions operating within the EU must therefore navigate the interplay between AML/CFT data retention requirements and strict data privacy regulations, ensuring that data is retained only for legitimate AML/CFT purposes and for the prescribed periods.

In the United Kingdom, the Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on Payer) Regulations 2017 (MLRs 2017) transpose the EU AML Directives into national law, establishing comprehensive requirements for financial institutions and other obliged entities. Regulation 40, 'Retention of documents and information,' mirrors the provisions of the EU Directives. It mandates that relevant persons must keep: (a) a copy of the documents and information obtained for the purpose of customer due diligence measures; and (b) supporting records (consisting of the original documents or copies) in respect of a transaction which is subject to customer due diligence measures. The retention period specified is five years from the date on which the business relationship ends or the date on which the occasional transaction is completed. Regulation 41, 'Data protection,' further elaborates on the handling of retained data, particularly personal data. It states that personal data obtained for the purposes of these Regulations may only be processed for the prevention of money laundering or terrorist financing. It also stipulates that such data must not be retained for longer than is necessary for those purposes, with the five-year period serving as the general maximum unless a longer period is justified and proportionate to the prevention of money laundering or terrorist financing. Any retention beyond five years must be reviewed annually to determine if it remains necessary. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), as a primary supervisor for many financial institutions in the UK, provides detailed guidance on these regulations, emphasizing the need for robust record-keeping systems that allow for swift retrieval of information, proper identification of beneficial owners, and a clear audit trail of all CDD actions and transaction monitoring activities. The overall objective across these jurisdictions is to provide authorities with the necessary tools to investigate and prosecute financial crimes, while obliging financial institutions to act as gatekeepers through diligent record-keeping.

특정금융정보법 제5조의4(금융회사등의 금융거래등 정보의 보유기간 등) ① 금융회사등은 제4조, 제4조의2, 제5조의2 및 제5조의3에 따른 의무이행(이하 이 조에서 “의무이행”이라 한다)과 관련된 다음 각 호의 자료 및 정보를 금융거래등의 관계가 종료한 때부터 5년간 보존하여야 한다. <개정 2020. 3. 24.>

1. 제4조 및 제4조의2에 따른 보고와 관련된 다음 각 목의 자료

가. 금융거래등 상대방의 실지명의(實地名義)를 확인할 수 있는 자료

나. 보고 대상이 된 금융거래등 자료

다. 금융회사등이 제4조제3항에 따라 의심되는 합당한 근거를 기록한 자료

2. 제5조의2제1항 각 호에 따른 고객확인자료

3. 제5조의3제1항 각 호에 따른 송금인 및 수취인에 관한 정보

4. 그 밖에 의무이행과 관련하여 금융정보분석원장이 정하여 고시하는 자료

② 제1항 각 호 외의 부분에서 “금융거래등의 관계가 종료한 때”의 기준은 다음 각 호의 날로 한다. <개정 2020. 3. 24.>

1. 제2조제2호가목의 경우에는 금융회사등과 고객 사이에 모든 채권채무관계가 종료한 날

2. 제2조제2호나목에서 규정하는 파생상품시장에서의 거래의 경우에는 거래종료사유 발생으로 거래종료일이 도래한 날. 다만, 고객의 계좌가 개설되어 있는 경우에는 그 계좌가 폐쇄된 날로 본다.

3. 제2조제2호다목의 경우에는 카지노사업자와 고객 사이에 카지노거래로 인한 채권채무관계를 정산한 날

4. 제2조제2호라목의 경우에는 가상자산사업자와 고객 사이에 가상자산거래로 인한 채권채무관계를 정산한 날

5. 그 밖의 금융거래등의 경우에는 대통령령으로 정하는 날

③ 제1항에 따른 보존의 방법, 장소 등 그 밖에 필요한 사항은 대통령령으로 정한다.

[본조신설 2019. 1. 15.]

자금세탁방지 및 공중협박자금조달금지에 관한 업무규정 제85조(보존대상) ① 금융회사등이 고객확인기록과 관련하여 보존해야 할 자료는 다음 각 호와 같다. 

1. 고객(대리인, 실제소유자 포함)에 대한 고객확인서, 실명확인증표 사본 또는 고객신원정보를 확인하거나 검증하기 위해 확보한 자료 

2. 고객신원정보 외에 금융거래의 목적 및 성격을 파악하기 위해 추가로 확인한 자료 

3. 고객확인을 위한 내부승인 관련 자료 

개인정보보호법 제5조(국가 등의 책무) ① 국가와 지방자치단체는 개인정보의 목적 외 수집, 오용ㆍ남용 및 무분별한 감시ㆍ추적 등에 따른 폐해를 방지하여 인간의 존엄과 개인의 사생활 보호를 도모하기 위한 시책을 강구하여야 한다.

② 국가와 지방자치단체는 제4조에 따른 정보주체의 권리를 보호하기 위하여 법령의 개선 등 필요한 시책을 마련하여야 한다.

③ 국가와 지방자치단체는 만 14세 미만 아동이 개인정보 처리가 미치는 영향과 정보주체의 권리 등을 명확하게 알 수 있도록 만 14세 미만 아동의 개인정보 보호에 필요한 시책을 마련하여야 한다. <신설 2023. 3. 14.>

④ 국가와 지방자치단체는 개인정보의 처리에 관한 불합리한 사회적 관행을 개선하기 위하여 개인정보처리자의 자율적인 개인정보 보호활동을 존중하고 촉진ㆍ지원하여야 한다. <개정 2023. 3. 14.>

⑤ 국가와 지방자치단체는 개인정보의 처리에 관한 법령 또는 조례를 적용할 때에는 정보주체의 권리가 보장될 수 있도록 개인정보 보호 원칙에 맞게 적용하여야 한다. <개정 2023. 3. 14.>

개인정보보호법 제16조(개인정보의 수집 제한) ① 개인정보처리자는 제15조제1항 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하여 개인정보를 수집하는 경우에는 그 목적에 필요한 최소한의 개인정보를 수집하여야 한다. 이 경우 최소한의 개인정보 수집이라는 입증책임은 개인정보처리자가 부담한다.

② 개인정보처리자는 정보주체의 동의를 받아 개인정보를 수집하는 경우 필요한 최소한의 정보 외의 개인정보 수집에는 동의하지 아니할 수 있다는 사실을 구체적으로 알리고 개인정보를 수집하여야 한다. <신설 2013. 8. 6.>

③ 개인정보처리자는 정보주체가 필요한 최소한의 정보 외의 개인정보 수집에 동의하지 아니한다는 이유로 정보주체에게 재화 또는 서비스의 제공을 거부하여서는 아니 된다. <개정 2013. 8. 6.>

개인정보보호법 제18조(개인정보의 목적 외 이용ㆍ제공 제한) ① 개인정보처리자는 개인정보를 제15조제1항에 따른 범위를 초과하여 이용하거나 제17조제1항 및 제28조의8제1항에 따른 범위를 초과하여 제3자에게 제공하여서는 아니 된다. <개정 2020. 2. 4., 2023. 3. 14.>

② 제1항에도 불구하고 개인정보처리자는 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 경우에는 정보주체 또는 제3자의 이익을 부당하게 침해할 우려가 있을 때를 제외하고는 개인정보를 목적 외의 용도로 이용하거나 이를 제3자에게 제공할 수 있다. 다만, 제5호부터 제9호까지에 따른 경우는 공공기관의 경우로 한정한다. <개정 2020. 2. 4., 2023. 3. 14.>

1. 정보주체로부터 별도의 동의를 받은 경우

2. 다른 법률에 특별한 규정이 있는 경우

3. 명백히 정보주체 또는 제3자의 급박한 생명, 신체, 재산의 이익을 위하여 필요하다고 인정되는 경우

4. 삭제 <2020. 2. 4.>

Beyond the transatlantic regulatory landscapes, other prominent financial hubs globally have also established rigorous AML/CFT data retention requirements, often drawing inspiration from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Recommendations, which serve as the international standard. These jurisdictions ensure that financial institutions maintain comprehensive records to facilitate investigations, support ongoing risk assessments, and demonstrate compliance with national and international obligations. The emphasis remains on the retention of customer due diligence (CDD) information, transaction records, and any internal analyses related to suspicious activities.

In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issues specific notices to financial institutions outlining their AML/CFT obligations. For banks, MAS Notice 626, titled 'Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism – Banks,' is a cornerstone. Paragraph 11 of MAS Notice 626 details the record-keeping requirements. It mandates that a bank must keep records, for a period of at least five years, of: (a) all transactions, both domestic and international; (b) the information obtained through its CDD measures; and (c) any reports made to the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office (STRO). The five-year retention period commences from the date on which the business relationship with the customer is terminated, or, in the case of an occasional transaction, from the date of the transaction. For transactions that do not form part of a business relationship, the five-year period runs from the date of the transaction. The Notice specifies that records must be sufficient to permit the reconstruction of individual transactions and to provide evidence for the prosecution of criminal activity. This includes, but is not limited to, copies of identification documents, account files, business correspondence, and transaction records such as payment orders, swift messages, and account statements. Furthermore, banks are expected to maintain records in a manner that allows for timely retrieval by the MAS or other competent authorities. The MAS places a strong emphasis on the integrity and security of these records, requiring banks to implement appropriate measures to protect against unauthorized access, alteration, or destruction. The overarching goal is to ensure that a comprehensive audit trail exists for all financial activities, enabling effective oversight and enforcement against money laundering and terrorist financing. Compliance with these data retention provisions is a critical component of a bank's overall AML/CFT framework, subject to regular inspection and audit by the MAS.

In Japan, the Financial Services Agency (FSA) oversees the implementation of AML/CFT measures, primarily based on the Act on Prevention of Transfer of Criminal Proceeds (APTCP). While the APTCP sets out the core legal framework, the FSA issues detailed guidelines and supervisory policies for various financial sectors, including banks, securities firms, and insurance companies. These guidelines often elaborate on the requirements for customer identification, transaction monitoring, and record-keeping, aligning with FATF Recommendations. Japanese financial institutions are generally required to retain records relating to customer identification and transaction details for a minimum of seven to ten years. Specifically, under the APTCP and related ordinances, financial institutions must retain the following types of information: (a) customer identification data, including copies of identification documents, for seven years from the termination of the business relationship; and (b) transaction records, including transaction details, for seven years from the date of the transaction. For certain types of records, such as those pertaining to suspicious transactions or complex transactions, the retention period may be extended or subject to specific requirements. The purpose of these extended retention periods, compared to the standard five years in some other jurisdictions, is to provide a longer historical view for investigative bodies to trace complex financial crimes, which often span multiple years. The FSA's guidelines emphasize the need for financial institutions to implement robust systems for managing and archiving these records, ensuring their accuracy, completeness, and accessibility. This includes maintaining records of the beneficial ownership information obtained during the CDD process, which is crucial for uncovering illicit financial networks. The records must be kept in a manner that allows them to be easily retrieved and presented to supervisory authorities or law enforcement agencies upon request. Furthermore, Japanese regulations often require financial institutions to retain records of their internal analyses and decisions regarding suspicious transactions, providing a transparent audit trail of their AML/CFT compliance efforts. The stringent data retention requirements in Japan underscore a commitment to combating financial crime by ensuring that a thorough historical record is available to support enforcement actions and regulatory oversight, thereby strengthening the integrity of the financial system against the threats of money laundering and terrorist financing.

In the United States, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX) significantly strengthened requirements pertaining to **External Audit** and corporate governance for publicly traded companies. Specifically, Section 302 mandates management certification of financial reports, while Section 404 requires management to establish and maintain an adequate internal control structure and procedures for **Financial Reporting**, which is then subject to independent auditor attestation. The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB), established by SOX, oversees the audits of public companies to protect investors, ensuring the quality and integrity of audit reports. **Audit Eligibility** for firms performing these engagements is strictly regulated by the PCAOB, including registration requirements and ongoing quality control standards. Any significant **Organizational Change**, such as a merger, acquisition, or spin-off, necessitates a thorough review of the entity's **Financial Reporting** obligations and the potential impact on the scope and timing of its **External Audit**. Entities undergoing such changes must ensure compliance with SEC filing requirements, including timely updates to their **Establishment Registration** details, which can directly affect their audit cycles and reporting periods. 

Within the European Union, the Audit Directive (2014/56/EU) and the Audit Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 537/2014) establish a common framework for statutory audits of public-interest entities (PIEs). These regulations impose stringent requirements concerning auditor independence, rotation, and public oversight of the **External Audit** function. For example, Article 17 of the Audit Regulation mandates rotation of the key audit partner after a maximum period of five years. MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU) and MiFIR (Regulation (EU) No 600/2014) impose comprehensive organizational and operational requirements on investment firms, directly impacting their internal controls and **Financial Reporting** processes, which are subsequently subject to **External Audit**. The **Audit Eligibility** of firms to conduct statutory audits of PIEs is subject to authorization and oversight by national competent authorities. Furthermore, any substantial **Organizational Change** within a regulated entity, such as a change of legal form or a significant restructuring, often requires prior notification to or approval from the relevant national regulator, affecting its **Establishment Registration** status and potentially triggering specific audit procedures to ensure continuity and compliance with **Financial Reporting** standards.

공인회계사법 제2조(직무범위) 공인회계사는 타인의 위촉에 의하여 다음 각호의 직무를 행한다.
1. 회계에 관한 감사ㆍ감정ㆍ증명ㆍ계산ㆍ정리ㆍ입안 또는 법인설립등에 관한 회계

2. 세무대리

3. 제1호 및 제2호에 부대되는 업무

공인회계사법 제21조(직무제한) ①공인회계사는 다음 각호의 1에 해당하는 자에 대한 재무제표(「주식회사 등의 외부감사에 관한 법률」 제2조에 따른 聯結財務諸表를 포함한다. 이하 같다)를 감사하거나 증명하는 직무를 행할 수 없다. <개정 2003. 12. 11., 2005. 7. 29., 2017. 10. 31., 2020. 5. 19.>

1. 자기 또는 배우자가 임원이나 그에 준하는 직위(財務에 관한 事務의 責任있는 擔當者를 포함한다)에 있거나, 과거 1년 이내에 그러한 직위에 있었던 자(會社를 포함한다. 이하 이 條에서 같다)

2. 자기 또는 배우자가 그 직원이거나 과거 1년 이내에 직원이었던 사람(배우자의 경우 재무에 관한 사무를 수행하는 직원으로 한정한다)

3. 제1호 및 제2호외에 자기 또는 배우자와 뚜렷한 이해관계가 있어서 그 직무를 공정하게 행하는 데 지장이 있다고 인정되어 대통령령으로 정하는 자

② 공인회계사는 특정 회사(해당 회사가 다른 회사와 「주식회사 등의 외부감사에 관한 법률」 제2조제3호에 따른 지배ㆍ종속 관계에 있어 연결재무제표를 작성하는 경우 그 다른 회사를 포함한다)의 재무제표를 감사하거나 증명하는 업무를 수행하는 계약을 체결하고 있는 기간 중에는 해당 회사에 대하여 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 업무를 할 수 없다. <개정 2016. 3. 29., 2017. 10. 31.>

1. 회계기록과 재무제표의 작성

2. 내부감사업무의 대행

3. 재무정보체제의 구축 또는 운영

4. 자산ㆍ자본, 그 밖의 권리 등(이하 “자산등”이라 한다)을 매도 또는 매수하기 위한 다음 각 목의 업무(부실채권의 회수를 목적으로 대통령령으로 정하는 사항은 제외한다)

가. 자산등에 대한 실사ㆍ재무보고ㆍ가치평가

나. 자산등의 매도ㆍ매수거래 또는 계약의 타당성에 대한 의견제시

5. 인사 및 조직 등에 관한 지원업무

6. 재무제표에 계상되는 보험충당부채 금액 산출과 관련되는 보험계리업무

7. 민ㆍ형사 소송에 대한 자문업무

8. 자금조달ㆍ투자 관련 알선 및 중개업무

9. 중요한 자산의 처분 및 양도, 지배인의 선임 또는 해임 등 경영에 관한 의사결정으로서 임원이나 이에 준하는 직위의 역할에 해당하는 업무

10. 그 밖에 재무제표의 감사 또는 증명업무와 이해상충의 소지가 있는 것으로서 대통령령으로 정하는 업무

③ 제2항의 공인회계사는 같은 항 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 업무 외의 업무는 내부통제절차 등 대통령령으로 정하는 절차에 따라 할 수 있다. <개정 2016. 3. 29.>

세무사법 제2조(세무사의 직무) 세무사는 납세자 등의 위임을 받아 다음 각 호의 행위 또는 업무(이하 “세무대리”라 한다)를 수행하는 것을 그 직무로 한다. <개정 2011. 5. 2., 2016. 1. 19., 2017. 12. 19.>


1. 조세에 관한 신고ㆍ신청ㆍ청구(과세전적부심사청구, 이의신청, 심사청구 및 심판청구를 포함한다) 등의 대리(「개발이익환수에 관한 법률」에 따른 개발부담금에 대한 행정심판청구의 대리를 포함한다)

2. 세무조정계산서와 그 밖의 세무 관련 서류의 작성

3. 조세에 관한 신고를 위한 장부 작성의 대행

4. 조세에 관한 상담 또는 자문

5. 세무관서의 조사 또는 처분 등과 관련된 납세자 의견진술의 대리

6. 「부동산 가격공시에 관한 법률」에 따른 개별공시지가 및 단독주택가격ㆍ공동주택가격의 공시에 관한 이의신청의 대리

7. 해당 세무사가 작성한 조세에 관한 신고서류의 확인. 다만, 신고서류를 납세자가 직접 작성하였거나 신고서류를 작성한 세무사가 휴업하거나 폐업하여 이를 확인할 수 없으면 그 납세자의 세무 조정이나 장부 작성의 대행 또는 자문 업무를 수행하고 있는 세무사가 확인할 수 있다.

8. 「소득세법」 또는 「법인세법」에 따른 성실신고에 관한 확인

9. 그 밖에 제1호부터 제8호까지의 행위 또는 업무에 딸린 업무

Regulatory frameworks across leading financial jurisdictions frequently impose stringent limitations on the equity investments made by financial institutions, primarily to safeguard financial stability, prevent undue concentration of power, and mitigate systemic risk. In the United States, for instance, the **Investment Company Act of 1940** (15 U.S.C. § 80a-1 et seq.) contains provisions designed to regulate investment companies and, indirectly, to influence how other financial entities interact with them. Specifically, **Section 12(d)** of the Act outlines restrictions on the acquisition of shares of other investment companies by registered investment companies. While primarily aimed at preventing fund-of-funds abuses, the underlying principle of preventing excessive control or complex ownership structures resonates across broader regulatory concerns regarding institutional investments. Furthermore, the **Bank Holding Company Act of 1956** (12 U.S.C. § 1841 et seq.) and its implementing regulations, such as the Federal Reserve Board’s **Regulation Y** (12 CFR Part 225), significantly restrict the non-banking activities and equity investments of bank holding companies and their subsidiaries. These rules generally limit a bank holding company’s ability to own or control more than 5% of the voting shares of a company engaged in activities not deemed “closely related to banking,” requiring prior Federal Reserve approval for certain acquisitions or investments that exceed specified thresholds or result in control. This framework is crucial for maintaining the separation of banking and commerce and for ensuring that taxpayer-backed financial institutions do not engage in excessively speculative or risky ventures. A more recent and prominent example is the **Volcker Rule**, codified in **Section 619 of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act** (12 U.S.C. § 1851). This rule prohibits banking entities from engaging in proprietary trading and from acquiring or retaining any equity, partnership, or other ownership interest in, or sponsoring, a hedge fund or private equity fund, subject to certain exceptions. The Volcker Rule directly addresses concerns about financial institutions taking on excessive risk through speculative investments, thereby protecting the stability of the financial system. 

In the European Union, the **Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR)** (Regulation (EU) No 575/2013) and the **Capital Requirements Directive (CRD IV)** (Directive 2013/36/EU), now updated by **CRR II** (Regulation (EU) 2019/876) and **CRD V** (Directive (EU) 2019/878), establish prudential requirements for credit institutions and investment firms. These instruments contain rules on large exposures and qualifying holdings, which directly impact a financial institution's ability to make significant equity investments in other entities. For instance, Article 395 of the CRR sets limits on large exposures, generally restricting an institution’s exposure to a single client or group of connected clients to 25% of its eligible capital. While not solely focused on equity, this can limit the size of a controlling or substantial equity stake. Furthermore, Article 46 of the CRR outlines deductions from Common Equity Tier 1 capital for certain holdings, including significant investments in other financial sector entities, effectively discouraging excessive cross-holdings. The **Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive (AIFMD)** (Directive 2011/61/EU) regulates managers of alternative investment funds (AIFs) and, while primarily focused on the management of third-party assets, it indirectly influences investment strategies and risk management practices, including potential limits on leverage and certain types of investments, especially when prudential regulators assess the overall risk profile of a financial institution that also operates as an AIFM. 

The United Kingdom, post-Brexit, largely retains similar principles through the **FCA Handbook** and **PRA Rulebook**. The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) imposes specific rules on banks, building societies, and insurers, including requirements for capital adequacy and limits on large exposures. For insurers, **Solvency II** (retained EU law framework, now implemented via the PRA Rulebook) imposes detailed requirements on the valuation of assets and liabilities, own funds, and capital requirements, including specific rules on asset allocation and diversification. These rules inherently constrain the types and concentrations of equity investments insurers can make to ensure policyholder protection and financial stability. For example, the PRA's **Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP)** requires firms to assess their own risks, including concentration risks arising from large equity holdings, and to hold adequate capital against them. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) also maintains rules under its **Conduct of Business Sourcebook (COBS)** and **Systems and Controls (SYSC)**, which, while focusing on investor protection and governance, indirectly influence the types of investments financial institutions can undertake by demanding robust risk management and due diligence processes. The UK’s regulatory approach consistently emphasizes the need for financial institutions to manage their investment exposures prudently, preventing concentrations that could pose risks to their solvency or the broader financial system.

Continuing the global perspective on financial institution investment limits, supervisory authorities in Asia also implement robust frameworks to ensure financial stability and prevent systemic risks. In Singapore, the **Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)**, acting as the central bank and integrated financial regulator, imposes strict controls on financial institutions' investments. The **Banking Act 1970** (Cap. 19) is a cornerstone, particularly concerning substantial shareholdings in banks and other financial institutions. Sections 15B and 15C of the Banking Act require prior approval from the MAS for any person to become a substantial shareholder (typically holding 5% or more of the shares) of a bank incorporated in Singapore. This approval process involves a rigorous assessment of the applicant's financial standing, reputation, and potential impact on the bank's governance and stability, effectively controlling the entry of significant investors, including other financial institutions. Furthermore, MAS Notices provide detailed prudential requirements. For instance, **MAS Notice 639 (Limits on Exposure to a Single Counterparty and to Related Parties)** sets limits on the aggregate exposure of a bank to any single counterparty or group of connected counterparties. While not exclusively targeting equity investments, a substantial equity holding in another entity would contribute to this exposure, thereby limiting the scale of such investments for prudential reasons. **MAS Notice 1003 (Risk-Based Capital Adequacy Requirements for Banks Incorporated in Singapore)** incorporates Basel III standards, requiring banks to maintain adequate capital for their risk-weighted assets, which includes capital charges for equity exposures, thus indirectly influencing the volume and risk profile of equity investments. The **Securities and Futures Act 2001** (Cap. 289) also regulates investment companies and collective investment schemes, ensuring that financial institutions engaging in such activities adhere to stringent licensing and conduct requirements, promoting market integrity and investor protection. 

In Japan, the **Financial Services Agency (FSA)** oversees a comprehensive regulatory regime for financial institutions. The **Banking Act of Japan** (Act No. 59 of 1981) contains specific provisions limiting banks' equity investments. **Article 16-2** of the Banking Act generally prohibits a bank from holding more than 5% of the voting shares of a company, with certain exceptions for financial subsidiaries or companies closely related to banking activities, which may require specific approvals. This limitation is a fundamental pillar of Japanese financial regulation, designed to prevent banks from exerting undue influence over non-financial corporations and to mitigate the risks associated with excessive cross-shareholdings, which historically contributed to financial instability. The FSA's interpretation and enforcement of these rules are rigorous, focusing on the prevention of conflicts of interest and the concentration of economic power. For investment vehicles, the **Act on Investment Trusts and Investment Corporations** (Act No. 198 of 1951) governs the establishment and operation of investment trusts and investment corporations (including J-REITs). This act sets out requirements for their structure, management, and disclosure, ensuring that financial institutions investing in or managing these vehicles adhere to specific regulatory standards. The **Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA)** (Act No. 25 of 1948) provides a broad framework for the regulation of financial instruments businesses, including securities firms and asset managers, and mandates strict disclosure requirements for public companies. While the FIEA primarily focuses on market conduct and investor protection, it complements the Banking Act by ensuring transparency and fair practices in the broader investment landscape, impacting how financial institutions execute and report their investment activities. The **Insurance Business Act** (Act No. 105 of 1995) also imposes prudential regulations on insurance companies, including rules related to asset management and investment limits, ensuring that insurers maintain sufficient solvency to meet their obligations to policyholders, often involving diversification requirements and restrictions on risky assets or concentrated holdings. Across these acts, the FSA’s objective is to foster a stable, efficient, and transparent financial system, managing risks arising from interconnectedness and concentrated ownership.

In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) regulates investment advisers, including those managing venture capital funds, primarily under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. While specific GP compensation structures are largely contractual, the Act mandates extensive disclosure to investors. For instance, Form ADV, Part 2A requires registered investment advisers to detail their advisory fees, including management fees and carried interest arrangements, ensuring transparency regarding compensation methods and potential conflicts of interest. Rule 206(4)-7 under the Advisers Act further obliges advisers to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of the Act, which inherently extends to the oversight of fee calculations and distributions. The SEC’s focus is on preventing fraud and ensuring fiduciary duty, meaning compensation must be clearly disclosed and not misleading.

Within the European Union, the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive (AIFMD, Directive 2011/61/EU) sets a comprehensive regulatory framework for Alternative Investment Fund Managers (AIFMs), which encompass many venture capital fund managers. Article 13 of AIFMD specifically addresses remuneration policies, requiring AIFMs to establish and maintain remuneration policies and practices that are consistent with sound and effective risk management and do not encourage excessive risk-taking. These provisions mandate that a significant portion of variable remuneration, such as carried interest, for identified staff (including GP principals) must be deferred over an appropriate period and subject to clawback provisions, aligning incentives with long-term fund performance and investor interests. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), post-Brexit, largely retains these principles under its SYSC rules, emphasizing robust governance and conflict management around remuneration.

여신전문금융업법 제44조(신기술사업투자조합)

1. 개인투자조합

2. 벤처투자조합

3. 「여신전문금융업법」 제2조제14호의5에 따른 신기술사업투자조합(이하 “신기술사업투자조합”이라 한다)

4. 「산업발전법」 제20조에 따른 기업구조개선 기관전용 사모집합투자기구

5. 「자본시장과 금융투자업에 관한 법률」 제9조제19항제1호에 따른 기관전용 사모집합투자기구

6. 「농림수산식품투자조합 결성 및 운용에 관한 법률」 제13조에 따른 농식품투자조합

7. 그 밖에 중소벤처기업부장관이 정하여 고시하는 자

③ 한국벤처투자는 벤처투자 활성화 등 정책 목적에 따라 모태조합의 자산을 관리ㆍ운용하여야 한다.

④ 모태조합의 존속기간은 대통령령으로 정하는 기간으로 하며, 그 밖에 모태조합의 관리ㆍ운용 등에 필요한 사항은 대통령령으로 정한다.

⑤ 중소벤처기업부장관은 모태조합이 출자한 개인투자조합 또는 벤처투자조합에 대해서는 제13조제1항 및 제2항, 제51조제1항 및 제2항에도 불구하고 투자비율을 달리 정할 수 있다.

In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) regulates fund management companies, including those managing venture capital funds, under the Securities and Futures Act (SFA). Licensed Fund Management Companies (LFMCs) are subject to stringent capital, conduct, and disclosure requirements. While MAS does not prescribe specific GP compensation structures, it mandates that fund managers maintain robust internal controls and governance frameworks to manage conflicts of interest arising from compensation arrangements. Circular FMC 01/2018, for example, emphasizes the importance of sound remuneration practices that are transparent and aligned with the long-term interests of investors and the fund. Disclosure of management fees, performance fees, and carried interest to investors is critical, ensuring that all aspects of GP compensation are clearly communicated and understood, in line with the broader principles of investor protection and market integrity.

Similarly, in Japan, the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA) governs investment management businesses. Investment limited partnerships, a common vehicle for venture capital funds, operate under specific provisions of the FIEA. The General Partner's (GP) compensation, typically comprising management fees and carried interest (or "success fees"), is subject to disclosure requirements to investors. The Financial Services Agency (FSA) emphasizes that such compensation structures must be fair, transparent, and clearly defined in the partnership agreement, preventing undue advantage to the GP. Regulations focus on ensuring that remuneration policies do not create conflicts of interest detrimental to the limited partners and that all contractual terms, including those related to performance-based compensation, are fully understood by investors prior to commitment, upholding principles of investor protection and sound market practices.

In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) mandates extensive disclosure requirements for asset-backed securities (ABS) under Regulation AB (17 CFR part 229.1100 et seq.). This regulatory framework ensures investors receive comprehensive information regarding the characteristics of the underlying receivables, the transaction structure, and the servicer’s performance. A critical legal consideration in US securitization involves the "true sale" opinion, which establishes that the transfer of receivables from the originator to the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) legally removes the assets from the originator's bankruptcy estate, thereby safeguarding investors. This principle is vital for the integrity of the capital markets and the effective transfer of economic risk.

Across the European Union, the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II, Directive 2014/65/EU and Regulation (EU) No 600/2014) governs the provision of investment services and activities in financial instruments. While not directly regulating the assignment of specific underlying receivables, MiFID II significantly impacts the trading and distribution of securitized products containing such receivables. It imposes rigorous transparency obligations, best execution rules, and investor protection measures on investment firms. Similarly, the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) maintains a comprehensive regulatory regime, building on transposed EU law and domestic mandates. The FCA's rules, often found in its Handbook (e.g., SYSC for Systems and Controls or COBS for Conduct of Business), emphasize robust governance, risk management, and client asset protection for authorized firms operating within the financial ecosystem, including those facilitating the transfer or management of various financial claims and payment streams.

여신전문금융업법 제2조(정의) 이 법에서 사용하는 용어의 뜻은 다음과 같다. <개정 2010. 3. 12., 2012. 3. 21., 2015. 1. 20., 2015. 7. 31., 2016. 3. 29., 2018. 2. 21., 2025. 10. 1.> 
5. “신용카드가맹점”이란 다음 각 목의 자를 말한다.

가. 신용카드업자와의 계약에 따라 신용카드회원ㆍ직불카드회원 또는 선불카드소지자(이하 “신용카드회원등”이라 한다)에게 신용카드ㆍ직불(直拂)카드 또는 선불(先拂)카드(이하 “신용카드등”이라 한다)를 사용한 거래에 의하여 물품의 판매 또는 용역의 제공 등을 하는 자

나. 신용카드업자와의 계약에 따라 신용카드회원등에게 물품의 판매 또는 용역의 제공 등을 하는 자를 위하여 신용카드등에 의한 거래를 대행(代行)하는 자(이하 “결제대행업체”라 한다)

여신전문금융업법 제20조(매출채권의 양도금지 등) ① 신용카드가맹점은 신용카드에 따른 거래로 생긴 채권(신용카드업자에게 가지는 매출채권을 포함한다. 이하 이 항에서 같다)을 신용카드업자와 「은행법」에 따라 설립된 은행(「중소기업은행법」에 따라 설립된 중소기업은행과 「농업협동조합법」에 따라 설립된 농협은행을 포함한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다) 외의 자(이하 이 조에서 “신용카드업자등 외의 자”라 한다)에게 양도하여서는 아니 되고, 신용카드업자등 외의 자는 이를 양수하여서는 아니 된다. 다만, 신용카드가맹점이 신용카드업자에게 가지는 매출채권을 「자산유동화에 관한 법률」 제2조제1호에 따른 자산유동화를 위하여 양도하는 경우에는 신용카드가맹점은 신용카드에 따른 거래로 생긴 채권을 신용카드업자등 외의 자에게 양도할 수 있고, 신용카드업자등 외의 자도 이를 양수할 수 있다. <개정 2010. 3. 12., 2016. 3. 29.>

In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) regulates payment service providers under the Payment Services Act (PSA) of 2019. This comprehensive framework governs various activities, including account issuance, domestic and cross-border money transfer services, merchant acquisition, and e-money issuance. The PSA mandates licensing for specific payment services, focusing on safeguarding customer funds, mitigating money laundering and terrorism financing risks, and ensuring operational resilience of payment systems. While the PSA does not explicitly detail the assignability of underlying receivables from merchant transactions, it establishes the regulatory environment for how payment service providers manage, settle, and secure funds, indirectly influencing the nature and transferability of claims held by and against them. MAS's stringent expectations for governance, risk management, and capital adequacy apply broadly to licensed entities, impacting their operational structures and balance sheet management.

Similarly, Japan's Financial Services Agency (FSA) oversees payment service providers through its Payment Services Act. This Act regulates entities involved in funds transfer services, prepaid payment instruments, and other related activities, aiming to ensure the stability and efficiency of payment systems, protect users, and prevent illicit financial activities. Licensed payment service providers are subject to capital adequacy requirements, strict segregation of customer funds—often through trust accounts as specified in Article 43 of the Payment Services Act—and robust internal control systems. The FSA's regulatory framework prioritizes the transparency of payment flows and the security of transactions, ensuring that even if underlying financial claims are transferred or securitized, customer funds remain adequately protected and accessible.

In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) mandates comprehensive disclosure for investors holding significant stakes in publicly traded financial companies. Under Section 13(d) and 13(g) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and further detailed in SEC Rule 13d-3, any person or group beneficially owning more than 5% of a class of a company's voting equity securities must file a Schedule 13D or 13G. Within the European Union, the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II), specifically Article 10, mandates prior notification and approval from competent authorities for acquiring or increasing a "qualifying holding" in an investment firm. A qualifying holding is defined as a direct or indirect holding representing 10% or more of the capital or voting rights, or enabling significant influence over management. The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) and its Handbook (e.g., SUP 11), implements similar robust change in control requirements for financial companies, mandating approval for acquiring or increasing control above defined thresholds. These regulations collectively safeguard the sound and prudent management of regulated financial institutions.

나. 다음 각 1) 및 2)의 어느 하나에 해당하는 자(이하 “주요주주”라 한다)

1) 누구의 명의로 하든지 자기의 계산으로 금융회사의 의결권 있는 발행주식 총수의 100분의 10 이상의 주식(그 주식과 관련된 증권예탁증권을 포함한다)을 소유한 자

금융회사의 지배구조에 관한 법률 시행령 제4조(주요주주의 범위) 법 제2조제6호나목2)에서 “대통령령으로 정하는 자”란 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 자를 말한다.

In Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) imposes stringent regulatory oversight on substantial shareholders within financial institutions. Under the Banking Act 1970, Part IV, any person seeking to become a "substantial shareholder" in a bank (generally holding 5% or more of its shares or voting power) must obtain prior MAS approval. This requirement extends to any increase in such holdings, ensuring only fit and proper individuals or entities exert significant influence over financial companies. The Securities and Futures Act 2001 also defines "substantial shareholder" (Part VII, Section 81) for listed companies, mandating disclosure of holdings of 5% or more.

Japan's Financial Services Agency (FSA) similarly enforces regulations to ensure the stability and sound management of financial institutions. The Banking Act (銀行法), Article 2, defines a "Major Shareholder" (大株主) of a bank as a person holding 20% or more (or 50% or more, depending on context) of its voting rights, imposing specific duties and regulatory scrutiny. Furthermore, the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (金融商品取引法), Article 27-23, mandates filing a Large Shareholding Report when an investor acquires or disposes of shares exceeding 5% of a listed company's total issued shares, promoting transparency in capital markets and corporate governance.

Under the European Union's Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II, Directive 2014/65/EU), investment firms are subject to stringent requirements for the safeguarding of client assets, particularly for retail investors engaging in foreign securities transactions. Article 16(8) mandates firms to make adequate arrangements to safeguard clients’ ownership rights and prevent the use of client financial instruments for their own account. Similarly, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Client Assets Sourcebook (CASS) rules, specifically CASS 7, outline detailed obligations for firms holding client money and safe custody assets. In the United States, SEC Rule 15c3-3 (Customer Protection - Reserves and Custody of Securities) requires broker-dealers to maintain physical possession or control over customers' fully paid and excess margin securities. The 'delivery out' or transfer of foreign securities from a domestic investment firm to a foreign brokerage, initiated by a retail investor, necessitates adherence to these protective frameworks, ensuring proper record-keeping and minimizing operational risks during the transfer process.

자본시장과 금융투자업에 관한 법률 시행령 제184조(해외시장 거래 등) ① 법 제166조에 따라 일반투자자(금융위원회가 정하여 고시하는 전문투자자를 포함한다)는 해외 증권시장이나 해외 파생상품시장에서 외화증권 및 장내파생상품의 매매거래(외국 다자간매매체결회사에서의 거래를 포함한다. 이하 이 조에서 같다)를 하려는 경우에는 투자중개업자를 통하여 매매거래를 해야 한다. 다만, 외화증권을 매도하려는 경우로서 다음 각 호의 요건을 모두 충족하는 경우에는 투자중개업자를 통하지 않고 매매거래를 할 수 있다. <개정 2013. 8. 27., 2021. 2. 9., 2024. 3. 5.>

Similarly, within the European Union, the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II, Directive 2014/65/EU) and its accompanying delegated regulations impose stringent organisational requirements on investment firms. The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) echoes these principles through its Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls (SYSC) handbook, particularly SYSC 6 (Compliance and internal audit) and SYSC 7 (Risk control). Under the UK's Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR), specific responsibilities are assigned to Senior Managers, including those responsible for risk, reinforcing the need for clear lines of accountability and the avoidance of conflicts arising from Concurrent Duties (겸직 금지) that could compromise the integrity of the risk management function, especially in areas like Loan Review.

Principle 4.8 of the Code specifically addresses the roles of independent directors in overseeing management and engaging with stakeholders. While the Code does not strictly mandate the separation of the Board chairperson and CEO roles, it encourages companies to consider the appropriate balance and to clearly define the responsibilities of the Board chairperson in fostering effective board discussions and decision-making. The global financial landscape is characterized by an intricate web of regulatory requirements designed to safeguard consumer data, ensure market integrity, and combat illicit financial activities. In the United States, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) stands as a foundational pillar for financial privacy, mandating that financial institutions explain their information-sharing practices to customers and protect sensitive data. Specifically, the GLBA's Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) requires financial institutions to implement comprehensive information security programs to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of nonpublic personal information (NPI). This includes establishing administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect customer records and information. Such NPI often encompasses detailed financial transaction information and personal credit information, the handling of which is meticulously prescribed. Furthermore, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) enforces Regulation S-P, 'Privacy of Consumer Financial Information' (17 CFR Part 248), which applies to broker-dealers, investment companies, and investment advisers. Regulation S-P mirrors many GLBA provisions, requiring these entities to adopt policies and procedures to protect customer records and information, and to provide privacy notices to customers. The ongoing evolution of cyber threats has also led to state-level regulations, such as the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500). This regulation imposes stringent cybersecurity requirements on financial institutions operating in New York, including risk assessments, multi-factor authentication, incident response plans, and a notification duty for cybersecurity events. These frameworks collectively emphasize robust data governance, access controls, and encryption to shield customer data from unauthorized access or misuse, even in scenarios involving potential requests from governmental bodies under tax laws, where the scope and legality of such data sharing are carefully scrutinized against privacy protections.

Across the Atlantic, the European Union's regulatory framework is dominated by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), a comprehensive data protection law that sets a high bar for the processing of personal data, including financial transaction information and personal credit information. GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) applies extraterritorially, impacting any entity processing data of EU residents. Article 5 outlines core data processing principles, including lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, and confidentiality. Article 6 specifies the lawful bases for processing, such as consent, contractual necessity, legal obligation, or legitimate interests. When governmental bodies, akin to a National Tax Service, seek financial transaction information under national tax laws, financial institutions must ensure such requests align with a valid legal obligation under Article 6(1)(c) or a public interest task under Article 6(1)(e), and that the disclosure is proportionate and necessary. Article 32 mandates appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, while Articles 33 and 34 establish a strict notification duty for data breaches, requiring prompt reporting to supervisory authorities and, in high-risk cases, to affected data subjects. The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II), alongside its accompanying Regulation (MiFIR), while primarily focused on market transparency and investor protection, indirectly imposes significant data management requirements. MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU) Article 16 mandates robust organizational requirements for investment firms, including systems and controls for data recording and storage, particularly for client orders and transactions. Article 25 further specifies extensive record-keeping obligations for all services, transactions, and communications, generating vast quantities of financial transaction information that subsequently fall under GDPR's protective umbrella. The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), effective from 2025, will further enhance the EU's financial sector resilience against ICT-related disruptions and threats. DORA mandates comprehensive ICT risk management frameworks, incident reporting, digital operational resilience testing, and robust third-party risk management, all of which directly bolster the security and integrity of financial transaction information and personal credit information held by financial entities. The interaction between these regulations means that any request for data, even for tax purposes, must navigate a complex interplay of privacy, security, and operational resilience requirements.

In the United Kingdom, following its departure from the EU, the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 largely mirror the EU GDPR's provisions, maintaining a high standard for personal data protection. Financial institutions are subject to the same principles of lawfulness, fairness, and transparency for processing personal credit information and financial transaction information, including when responding to requests from HMRC (Her Majesty's Revenue and Customs) under specific tax laws. The notification duty for data breaches remains a critical compliance obligation, with reporting to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and affected individuals as required. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Handbook also imposes significant requirements through its Principles for Businesses (PRIN) and Systems and Controls (SYSC) chapters. PRIN 3 requires firms to take reasonable care to organize and control their affairs responsibly and effectively, with adequate risk management systems, which inherently includes data protection. SYSC 8, in particular, focuses on information security, requiring firms to establish, implement, and maintain adequate policies and procedures sufficient to ensure the security, integrity, and confidentiality of information. This extends to the secure handling of financial transaction information and personal credit information, ensuring that even legitimate requests, for example, from the National Tax Service equivalent under tax laws, are processed with appropriate safeguards and recorded diligently. The Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR), while primarily focusing on individual accountability, indirectly reinforces data governance by assigning clear responsibilities for risk management and control functions, including those related to data protection and cybersecurity, ensuring that senior leadership is accountable for the firm's compliance with these stringent data handling requirements and the timely execution of any notification duty.

신용정보의 이용 및 보호에 관한 법률 제3조의2(다른 법률과의 관계) ① 신용정보의 이용 및 보호에 관하여 다른 법률에 특별한 규정이 있는 경우를 제외하고는 이 법에서 정하는 바에 따른다.

② 개인정보의 보호에 관하여 이 법에 특별한 규정이 있는 경우를 제외하고는 「개인정보 보호법」에서 정하는 바에 따른다.

신용정보의 이용 및 보호에 관한 법률 제32조(개인신용정보의 제공ㆍ활용에 대한 동의) ⑦ 제6항 각 호에 따라 개인신용정보를 타인에게 제공하려는 자 또는 제공받은 자는 대통령령으로 정하는 바에 따라 개인신용정보의 제공 사실 및 이유 등을 사전에 해당 신용정보주체에게 알려야 한다. 다만, 대통령령으로 정하는 불가피한 사유가 있는 경우에는 인터넷 홈페이지 게재 또는 그 밖에 유사한 방법을 통하여 사후에 알리거나 공시할 수 있다. <개정 2011. 5. 19., 2015. 3. 11.>

신용정보의 이용 및 보호에 관한 법률 제35조(신용정보 이용 및 제공사실의 조회) ① 신용정보회사등은 개인신용정보를 이용하거나 제공한 경우 대통령령으로 정하는 바에 따라 다음 각 호의 구분에 따른 사항을 신용정보주체가 조회할 수 있도록 하여야 한다. 다만, 내부 경영관리의 목적으로 이용하거나 반복적인 업무위탁을 위하여 제공하는 경우 등 대통령령으로 정하는 경우에는 그러하지 아니하다.

1. 개인신용정보를 이용한 경우: 이용 주체, 이용 목적, 이용 날짜, 이용한 신용정보의 내용, 그 밖에 대통령령으로 정하는 사항

2. 개인신용정보를 제공한 경우: 제공 주체, 제공받은 자, 제공 목적, 제공한 날짜, 제공한 신용정보의 내용, 그 밖에 대통령령으로 정하는 사항

② 신용정보회사등은 제1항에 따라 조회를 한 신용정보주체의 요청이 있는 경우 개인신용정보를 이용하거나 제공하는 때에 제1항 각 호의 구분에 따른 사항을 대통령령으로 정하는 바에 따라 신용정보주체에게 통지하여야 한다.

③ 신용정보회사등은 신용정보주체에게 제2항에 따른 통지를 요청할 수 있음을 알려주어야 한다.

Continuing the global perspective on financial data protection, jurisdictions in Asia also maintain rigorous regulatory frameworks to safeguard sensitive information. In Singapore, the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) 2012 provides a comprehensive data protection regime applicable to all organizations, including financial institutions, handling personal data. The PDPA establishes nine key obligations: Consent, Purpose Limitation, Notification, Access and Correction, Accuracy, Protection, Retention Limitation, Transfer Limitation, and Accountability. Sections 13 to 16, specifically, require organizations to obtain consent for the collection, use, and disclosure of personal data, including financial transaction information and personal credit information, and to ensure that such processing is for reasonable purposes. This means that even when a governmental body, analogous to a National Tax Service, seeks data under specific tax laws, financial institutions must ensure that the disclosure aligns with one of the PDPA's exceptions to consent (e.g., for legal or regulatory requirements) and adheres to the purpose limitation principle. Section 24 of the PDPA outlines the mandatory notification duty in the event of a data breach, requiring organizations to assess the breach and, if it is notifiable, to inform the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) and affected individuals without undue delay. Furthermore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issues detailed Technology Risk Management (TRM) Guidelines, which set out expectations for financial institutions to manage technology risks, including cybersecurity and data protection. The MAS TRM Guidelines emphasize the need for robust information security measures, data integrity, and resilience against cyber threats, directly impacting how financial transaction information and personal credit information are stored, processed, and transmitted. These guidelines mandate regular risk assessments, implementation of strong access controls, encryption, and comprehensive incident response plans, ensuring that data is protected throughout its lifecycle, even when subject to requests under tax laws, thereby reinforcing the institution's notification duty to regulators and affected parties in case of security incidents.

Japan's regulatory landscape for financial data protection is primarily governed by the Act on Protection of Personal Information (APPI) and supplementary guidelines issued by the Financial Services Agency (FSA). The APPI (Act No. 57 of 2003) sets forth fundamental principles for the handling of personal information, including explicit provisions for financial institutions. Article 15 mandates that personal information, including sensitive financial transaction information and personal credit information, must be handled within the scope necessary to achieve a specified purpose of use. Article 17 requires entities to acquire personal information by appropriate means and not through deception or other illicit methods. Critically, Article 20 obliges organizations to take necessary and appropriate measures for the security management of personal data, including preventing leakage, loss, or damage, and for the supervision of employees and contractors handling such data. Article 23 governs the provision of personal data to third parties, generally requiring prior consent from the individual, with specific exceptions. This is particularly relevant when a governmental body, akin to a National Tax Service, requests financial information under tax laws; the disclosure must align with an exception or a specific legal mandate that overrides the consent requirement, and the institution must document the legal basis meticulously. In the event of a data breach, Article 26 and related guidelines establish a notification duty to the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC) and, in certain circumstances, to the affected data subjects, ensuring transparency and accountability. The FSA, as the primary regulator for financial institutions, issues comprehensive guidelines for the supervision of various financial business operators, which often elaborate on the APPI's requirements within the financial context. These guidelines emphasize the importance of robust internal control systems for information security management, including systems for preventing unauthorized access, ensuring data accuracy, and maintaining business continuity. They also stress the proper management of outsourcing risks, ensuring that third-party vendors handling financial transaction information and personal credit information adhere to equivalent data protection standards. These collective frameworks ensure that financial institutions in Japan maintain high standards for data privacy and security, even when faced with governmental requests under tax laws, and are prepared to fulfill their notification duty in the event of data security incidents, thereby upholding trust and regulatory compliance in the financial sector.

While the direct term 'Specially Related Person' (특수관계인) is not a statutory definition, analogous concepts are found in various rules. For instance, Item 404 of Regulation S-K mandates disclosure of 'related person transactions,' defined to include transactions between the registrant and any director, executive officer, nominee for director, or 5% shareholder, or their immediate family members. This framework aims to identify individuals or entities with the potential for undue influence or conflicts of interest. Furthermore, under the Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 2(a)(9) defines 'control' as the power to exercise a controlling influence over the management or policies of a company, generally presumed to exist with 25% ownership of voting securities, but also considering other factors. These provisions are crucial for entities, including those structured similarly to a 'Venture Investment Fund' (벤처투자조합), where significant investors, potentially analogous to a '유한책임조합원' (Limited Partner), might be deemed to exercise control or be a related person. In the European Union, the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II, Directive 2014/65/EU) and its accompanying delegated regulations, such as Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565, incorporate the concept of 'close links' (Article 4(1)(35) of MiFID II). This refers to a situation in which two or more natural or legal persons are linked by a 'control' relationship or by a 'participation' relationship, or where they are permanently linked to the same third person by a control relationship. Such definitions are critical in assessing governance structures and potential conflicts of interest within investment firms. Similarly, the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Handbook, particularly SYSC 4.1.2, requires firms to have robust governance arrangements. context:
The regulatory landscape for financial institutions across major global jurisdictions consistently emphasizes robust corporate governance, particularly concerning the concurrent positions held by executives and directors. This focus stems from the imperative to mitigate conflicts of interest, ensure sufficient time commitment, maintain independence, and prevent anti-competitive practices. Jurisdictions such as the United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom have developed intricate frameworks to address these concerns.

In the United States, the prevention of interlocking directorates, where the same person serves as a director or officer for multiple competing financial institutions, is a cornerstone of antitrust law. Section 8 of the Clayton Act (15 U.S.C. § 19) explicitly prohibits such interlocks between certain competing corporations, particularly those engaged in commerce. This prohibition is further elaborated and enforced by the Federal Reserve Board through its Regulation L (12 CFR Part 212), which applies to depository institutions. Regulation L specifies conditions under which an individual may serve as an officer or director of more than one depository organization and outlines exceptions, such as those for affiliated organizations or organizations not deemed 'competitors' under the statutory definition. The primary objective is to prevent concentrated power and information sharing that could lead to reduced competition. Beyond antitrust concerns, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and major stock exchanges like the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and NASDAQ impose stringent independence requirements for directors of listed companies, particularly for those serving on audit committees. For instance, Exchange Act Rule 10A-3 mandates that audit committee members be independent, prohibiting them from receiving any consulting, advisory, or other compensatory fee from the issuer or its subsidiaries, or being an affiliated person of the issuer. While not directly limiting the number of concurrent positions, the spirit of independence and the expectation of sufficient time commitment are inherent in these rules.

The European Union has significantly strengthened its corporate governance requirements for financial institutions, particularly through the Capital Requirements Directive V (CRD V, Directive (EU) 2019/878). Article 88 of CRD V, pertaining to the 'management body', introduces specific limits on the number of directorships that members of the management body of a financial institution may hold concurrently. For significant financial institutions, an individual may hold either one executive directorship and two non-executive directorships, or four non-executive directorships. These limits are designed to ensure that members of the management body can dedicate sufficient time to their responsibilities within the financial institution. Member States have the discretion to allow one additional non-executive directorship where the non-executive directorships are held in companies that are not financial undertakings. The European Banking Authority (EBA) further elaborates on these provisions through its 'Guidelines on internal governance' (EBA/GL/2021/05), which provide detailed guidance on the assessment of suitability, including the time commitment required for members of the management body and the management of actual or potential conflicts of interest arising from concurrent positions.

In the United Kingdom, following its departure from the EU, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) maintain a robust regulatory framework that largely aligns with the principles of CRD V and MiFID II. The Senior Managers and Certification Regime (SMCR), established under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) and implemented through the PRA Rulebook and FCA Handbook, places a strong emphasis on individual accountability, fitness, and propriety. While the UK does not always impose explicit numerical limits on concurrent directorships for all executives, the 'fitness and propriety' assessment for senior managers (as outlined in SYSC 5.1 and the PRA/FCA Statements of Principle and Code of Conduct for Senior Managers) inherently considers whether an individual has sufficient time, capacity, and integrity to perform their designated responsibilities effectively. Any concurrent position that could lead to a conflict of interest or compromise an individual's ability to dedicate adequate time to their primary role in a financial institution would be scrutinized under these rules. The FCA Handbook's SYSC 10 (Conflicts of Interest) also mandates firms to take all reasonable steps to identify, prevent, manage, and disclose conflicts of interest, which would include those potentially arising from executives holding positions in other entities.

금융회사의 지배구조에 관한 법률 제10조(겸직제한) ① 금융회사의 상근 임원은 다른 영리법인의 상시적인 업무에 종사할 수 없다. 다만, 다음 각 호의 어느 하나에 해당하는 경우에는 상시적인 업무에 종사할 수 있다.
